definition: Personal needs that support lifestyle, including eating, mobility, dressing, toileting, and personal hygiene. Self-dependence is fostered by ensuring the environment provides supplies and assistance to support self-performance.
Movement of a limb away from the midline of the body.
Movement of a limb toward the midline of the body.
The act of walking or moving from place to place. CNAs provide verbal prompts to guide ambulation toward desired locations and use gait/transfer belts to assist safely.
The heartbeat heard at the apex of the heart using a stethoscope, located at the 5th intercostal space at the midclavicular line.

The absence of disease-causing microorganisms. Medical asepsis (clean technique) reduces the number of pathogens and prevents their spread from one person or place to another. Surgical asepsis eliminates all microorganisms. 'Clean' means free of pathogenic organisms; 'dirty' means contaminated or soiled.
The inhalation of food, fluid, or foreign material into the airway, which can cause choking or pneumonia. Prevented by keeping the head of bed elevated at least 30-45 degrees during and after meals.

The force exerted by blood against the walls of the arteries. Recorded as systolic (contraction) over diastolic (relaxation) pressure. Normal adult range: less than 120/80 mmHg. Hypertension: 130/80 or higher. Hypotension: below 90/60. Use correct cuff size; place cuff 1 inch above the antecubital space.

The use of correct posture, balance, and movement to prevent injury when lifting, moving, or repositioning patients. Keep back straight, bend at knees, keep load close, avoid twisting, feet shoulder-width apart for wide base of support. Push/pull rather than lift when possible.
A flexible tube inserted into the body to drain fluids; a urinary (Foley) catheter drains urine from the bladder. Catheterized patients are at increased risk for urinary tract infections.
Permanent shortening and tightening of muscles or tendons causing deformity and limited range of motion, often resulting from prolonged immobility.

Also known as a pressure ulcer or bedsore; a wound caused by prolonged pressure on skin over bony prominences. Prevented by repositioning at least every 2 hours, keeping skin clean and dry, and not massaging reddened areas.
Difficulty breathing or shortness of breath. Report immediately; position patient in Fowler's position to ease breathing.
Swelling caused by excess fluid accumulation in body tissues. Weight change with swollen legs or feet is a warning sign to report (STOP and WATCH).
The ability to understand and share the feelings of another person; different from sympathy in that it involves perspective-taking. A key characteristic of an effective CNA.
Straightening of a joint, increasing the angle between bones.
Bending of a joint, decreasing the angle between bones.

A semi-sitting position where the head of the bed is raised 45-60 degrees. Semi-Fowler's is 30-45 degrees. High Fowler's is 90 degrees. Used to aid breathing and feeding. The best position during and after meals to prevent aspiration.

Also called a transfer belt; a belt worn by the resident so the nursing assistant can hold and support them during ambulation or transfers. Provides a secure grip around the patient's waist for safe movement.

The single most important method of preventing the spread of infection. Wash with soap and water for at least 20 seconds. Use alcohol-based sanitizer (at least 60% alcohol) when hands are not visibly soiled. Wash before/after patient contact, after removing gloves, before eating, after restroom use, before and after breaks, and before entering a clean supply room.
An emergency technique used to dislodge an object from the airway of a choking person using abdominal thrusts. Indicated when a resident has a blocked airway.
High blood pressure; defined as 130/80 mmHg or higher.
Low blood pressure; systolic reading below 90/60 mmHg. Orthostatic hypotension occurs when blood pressure drops upon standing.
The inability to control bladder (urinary) or bowel (fecal) function. Requires perineal care after each episode and use of moisture barriers to protect skin.
Measurement and recording of all fluids taken in (oral, IV) and all fluids expelled (urine, drainage) to monitor fluid balance. 8 oz = approximately 240 mL.

Practices used to prevent the spread of infection. Transmission-Based Precautions include: Airborne (N95 respirator, negative pressure room — TB, measles, chickenpox), Droplet (surgical mask — influenza, meningitis, mumps), and Contact (gown and gloves — MRSA, C. diff, gastrointestinal/skin/wound infections).
Side-lying position; used to relieve pressure on the back and sacrum.
A technique used to turn a patient as a unit, maintaining spinal alignment; used for patients with spinal injuries.
Failure to provide the standard of care that a reasonably prudent person would provide, resulting in harm to a patient.
Communication without words. How you feel about a person, assignment or task may be communicated nonverbally through: facial expressions, body language, posture, touch, and tone of voice.
Latin for 'nothing by mouth' (nil per os); a patient restriction from eating or drinking, often before surgery or procedures.
A surgically created opening (stoma) in the body to divert waste. A colostomy diverts stool; a urostomy diverts urine.

A microorganism (germ) that causes disease, including bacteria (TB, pneumonia, strep throat), viruses (influenza, common cold, herpes, HIV/AIDS), and fungi (athlete's foot, ringworm, yeast infections). A pathogen that spreads easily from person to person is contagious.

Equipment worn to minimize exposure to hazards, including gloves, goggles, face shields, masks, laboratory coats, gowns, shoe covers, and surgical caps. Donning order: Gown → Mask → Goggles/Face shield → Gloves. Removing order: Gloves → Gown → Mask.
Lying face down on the abdomen.

A non-invasive measurement of oxygen saturation in the blood (SpO2). Normal range: 95-100%. Below 90% is a medical emergency — report immediately. Poor circulation and nail polish can affect readings.
The full movement potential of a joint. Active ROM is performed by the patient; Passive ROM (PROM) is performed by the CNA. PROM stands for Passive Range of Motion.

The process of breathing; one respiration = one inhalation + one exhalation. Normal adult rate: 12-20 breaths/minute. Apnea = absence of breathing. Count respirations after taking pulse so patient is unaware.

Devices used to limit patient movement; require a physician order, patient/family consent, and regular monitoring. The least restrictive method must always be tried first. Check every 30 minutes; release and reposition at least every 2 hours. Never tie to side rails.

The procedures, actions, and processes a healthcare worker is permitted to perform based on their training, experience, and licensure. CNAs work under supervision of licensed nurses (RN/LPN) and must never perform tasks outside their scope of practice.
Lying flat on the back (face up).

A vital sign measuring body heat. Normal oral temperature: 98.6°F (37°C). Routes: Oral (most common), Rectal (most accurate, 1° higher), Axillary (armpit, 1° lower), Tympanic (ear), Temporal (forehead). Wait 10-20 minutes after the resident has had a cold or hot drink before taking oral temperature. Report above 100.4°F (fever).
See Gait Belt; worn by the resident so the nursing assistant can hold and support them. Used when assisting patients with walking or transferring.
Position where the body is laid flat on the back with the feet elevated higher than the head; used in some emergency situations.

An infection in any part of the urinary system. One of the most common healthcare-associated infections. Common in catheterized patients; symptoms include burning, frequency, and cloudy or dark urine. Prevented by proper perineal care (front to back for females) and good hand hygiene.

A biopsychosocial model that assists staff in planning care for residents. Supports remaining abilities and caring relationships. Each letter represents a level in the hierarchy of needs: Biological, Activities of Daily Living, Societal, Inter-personal, Creative, Symbolic.
Basic needs for: food, water, oxygen, safety, rest, and human stimulation. When met, fosters self-preservation — the resident is physically cared for and safe.

The need for unique personal identity, privacy, and the resident's place in society. When met, fosters self-identity through privacy, affiliation with groups, culture, family customs, education, and resident selection of associations.

The need for connection with others: love and belonging. When met, fosters self-esteem through social role expression, supports interpersonal and social abilities, promotes social confidence, and creates an atmosphere of caring.

The need for personal expression, problem solving opportunities, and meaningful activity that brings joy to the resident's life. When met, fosters self-expression through independent activity, humor, creativity, and use of talents and skills.

The need for expression of beliefs, hopes, dreams, values, and autonomy (ability to control important aspects of life). Includes sense of peace according to the resident's belief in the meaning of life. When met, fosters self-actualization through hopefulness and spiritual support.

The particular character, or aggregate of qualities, that distinguishes one person or thing from others; sole and personal nature. Proper care requires establishing a relationship based upon mutual respect and understanding of each resident as an individual human being with personal needs and expectations.

A genuine passion to be open and flexible with others; to accept differences and build on similarities; to be willing to learn from others as cultural informants. The CNA's commitment to care for all residents regardless of their cultural values, beliefs, customs, or practices.

An active process of listening not only to words but also to how they are expressed. Requires effort, skills, and practice. Components include: Encouraging, Clarifying, Restating, Reflecting, Summarizing, and Validating. Use your ears and eyes; people provide information about their feelings and emotions as well as conveying a message.

The oral or written exchange of information. Has 4 parts: the speaker or sender, the message being sent, the listener or receiver of the message, and feedback. Choose words that are positive, non-threatening, and understood by the resident.

A condition in which the resident is able to hear and, in most cases, understand you, but is unable to speak. The resident may try to answer but the words may not come, or they may use a word that does not fit. Allow nonverbal communication such as gestures, writing, pointing, or picture boards.

A relationship between an individual who suffers from a disability or discomfort (resident) and a practitioner (caregiver) who possesses a specific technical skill or knowledge and who occupies a recognized role. Goals: to promote communication of distressing thoughts/feelings, assist with problem solving for daily living, and promote self-care and independence.

A healthcare worker who serves as the eyes, ears, and hands of the licensed nurses. Responsible for basic day-to-day care of residents including: bathing, dressing, hair care, mouth care, nail care, shaving, toileting, vital signs and weight, food service, feeding, bed making, moving the resident, environmental cleanliness, and reporting observations.

A written account of a person's illness and response to treatment and care. It provides a way for the health team to communicate information about the person. The record is a permanent, legal document. Documentation types include: MDS, ADL Documentation, Care Plan, Meal Consumption Record, Toileting Schedule, Bowel Record, Turning and Repositioning Record.

A complex form completed upon admission and at various times during a resident's stay at the nursing home. Includes information about the care the resident requires and receives. The MDS is the universal assessment tool used in long-term care settings.

A written guide about the care a resident should receive. A communication tool used by staff to ensure the health team is giving the same care. Components include: Nursing Diagnosis, Goal, Measures or actions to achieve the goal, and Evaluation.

Interventions to Reduce Acute Care Transfers. A quality improvement program focusing on the management of acute change in resident condition. Includes clinical and educational tools and strategies for everyday practice in long-term care facilities. The Stop and Watch Early Warning Tool is used by CNAs to identify and communicate changes in residents.

An early warning tool used to identify changes in a resident's condition. STOP and WATCH acronym: Seems different than usual; Talks or communicates less; Overall needs more help; Pain - new or worsening/Participated less in activities; Ate less; No bowel movement in 3 days or diarrhea; Drank less; Weight change/swollen legs or feet; Agitated or nervous more than usual; Tired/weak/confused/drowsy; Change in skin color or condition; Help with walking/transferring/toileting more than usual.

Preserving the privacy of the residents in your care. All information related to residents is kept in strict confidence for use only by the care team. Breach of confidentiality is sharing information verbally or in written form with someone not on the care team or who does not have a release of information form. Confidential information includes: age, sex, race, religion, marital status, occupation, health information, SSN, insurance, lab results, MRI/CT scans, and any personal care.

Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act. Ensures the privacy of personal medical information shared with doctors, hospitals, and others who provide and pay for healthcare. Personal health information must remain confidential and cannot be shared without the individual's authorization. Applies to medical records on paper, in computers, and information communicated orally.

A tiny living organism that can be seen only through a microscope. Microorganisms are everywhere: in the air, on the objects we touch, and in our bodies. Pathogens are microorganisms that cause disease. Most pathogens grow best where there is warmth, moisture, darkness, a food source, and oxygen.

For an infection to occur, all 6 links must be present: (1) Infectious Agent — the pathogenic microorganism; (2) Reservoir — any place pathogens can live and multiply; (3) Portal of Exit — the opening a pathogen uses to leave the body; (4) Mode of Transmission — how infection is carried (contact, droplet, airborne, common vehicle, vector); (5) Portal of Entry — the point a pathogen enters the body; (6) Susceptible Host — a person whose defenses against infection are weakened. Breaking any link stops the infection.

Infections caused by bacteria resistant to many antibiotics. Examples include MRSA (Methicillin-Resistant Staphylococcus Aureus) and VRE (Vancomycin Resistant Enterococcus). These infections do not respond to traditional antibiotic therapy. Require Contact Precautions (gown and gloves).

Disease-causing microorganisms present in blood or body fluids. Examples: Hepatitis B (HBV), Hepatitis C (HCV), and Human Immunodeficiency Virus (HIV). Transmitted through sexual contact, sharing needles, needle stick injuries, and contact with infected blood on non-intact skin or mucous membranes. NOT spread by kissing, hugging, sneezing, coughing, food/water, or casual contact.

A serious disease caused by a virus that attacks the liver. Can cause lifelong infection, cirrhosis (scarring), liver cancer, liver failure, and death. About 30% of persons have no symptoms. When symptoms occur: jaundice, fatigue, abdominal pain, loss of appetite, nausea, vomiting, joint pain. Preventable by vaccination (3 injections: 2nd given 1 month after first, 3rd given 6 months after second). Vaccine available free to employees.

A serious disease caused by a virus that attacks the liver. Can lead to liver cancer, liver failure, or cirrhosis — irreversible and potentially fatal scarring of the liver. 80% of people have no symptoms; symptoms may not appear for 10-20 years. Symptoms: nausea/vomiting, diarrhea, loss of appetite, fatigue, pain over the liver, jaundice, dark-colored urine, pale stools.

Human Immunodeficiency Virus causes AIDS by infecting and damaging lymphocytes — white blood cells that fight infection. People may show no symptoms at time of infection; may take up to 10 years for symptoms to show. Symptoms: rapid weight loss, intense fatigue, swollen lymph nodes, persistent diarrhea, night sweats, pneumonia. Transmitted sexually, through needles, infected blood/organs, mother to infant.

The process of killing disease-causing microorganisms. Bleach is one commonly used disinfectant. Disinfection kills many, but not all, microorganisms. Cleaning (with soap/water or alcohol) is done first to remove large particles, followed by disinfection or sterilization.
The process of killing ALL microorganisms (both pathogens and non-pathogens) using very high temperatures with heat or steam under pressure. The machine used is called an autoclave.

A rigid container for needles, broken glass, safety razors, or other sharps used until filled to the line (about 3/4 full). The box is then locked, secured, and disposed of with biohazard/medical waste. Puncture resistant, labeled with the Biohazard symbol, color-coded in red, and leak-proof on sides and bottom.

Items contaminated with a resident's blood, body fluids, secretions, or excretions. Must be bagged in leak-proof plastic bags to remove from a resident's room. Regulated waste includes: liquid or semi-liquid blood, items contaminated with blood, items caked with blood, and contaminated sharps.
A device used to replace a missing part of the body.

The Occupational Safety and Health Administration is a federal government agency that makes rules to protect employees from hazards on the job. Mandates that employers have a written Exposure Plan to identify employees at risk and actions to take when an exposure incident occurs.

An infection acquired while in a healthcare setting. Most common types are urinary tract infections, surgical-site infections, pneumonia, or bloodstream infections. The single most important prevention measure is proper hand washing.

The respiratory disease caused by the virus SARS-CoV-2. Spreads primarily through person-to-person contact via respiratory particles (droplets and aerosols). Also capable of contact, droplet, and airborne transmission in healthcare settings. Symptoms include: fever or chills, new loss of taste/smell, cough, sore throat, shortness of breath, congestion, fatigue, nausea/vomiting, muscle aches, diarrhea, headache.

A person whose natural defenses against infection are weakened. A person's ability to resist infection relates to: age, nutritional status, stress, fatigue, medications, and presence of disease or injury. The elderly and those with diabetes, COPD, or renal disease are at higher risk.

Using the senses of sight, hearing, touch, and smell to collect information about a resident. Basic observations to report include: ability to respond, movement, pain or discomfort, skin condition, eyes/ears/nose/mouth, respirations, bowels and bladder, appetite, and ADLs.

Activities/Recreation Director: assesses and implements recreational needs. Administrator: planning/organizing/directing/supervising the facility. Dietician: assesses nutritional needs. LPN: provides direct care including medications under RN direction. Occupational Therapist: assists with ADL skills and adaptive equipment. Pharmacist: fills medication orders and monitors drug interactions. Physical Therapist: assists with musculoskeletal problems. Physician: diagnoses and treats diseases. RN: assesses, makes nursing diagnoses, plans and evaluates care. Social Worker: helps with social/emotional/environmental issues. Speech Therapist: treats speech, voice, communication, and swallowing disorders.

The overall well-being and life satisfaction of a resident in a care facility. Includes physical, mental, social, and spiritual dimensions. CNAs promote quality of life by honoring resident choices, maintaining dignity, supporting relationships, and providing person-centered care.

The degree to which healthcare services increase the likelihood of desired health outcomes and are consistent with professional standards. In nursing facilities, it encompasses clinical care, safety, dignity, and resident rights.

Care that respects and responds to individual resident preferences, needs, and values, ensuring they guide clinical decisions. Focuses on what matters most to the resident, not just clinical outcomes.

A care philosophy that addresses all dimensions of a person — physical, psychological, social, and spiritual. Recognizes that residents are more than their medical conditions. CNAs support the whole person by encouraging independence, honoring preferences, and supporting meaningful activities.

Federal and state mandated rights of nursing home residents, including: the right to dignity and respect, to be free from abuse and restraints, to privacy and confidentiality, to make choices about daily life, to participate in care planning, to voice grievances, to manage personal finances, and to have visitors.

Willful infliction of injury, unreasonable confinement, intimidation, or punishment that results in physical harm, pain, or mental anguish to a resident. Includes physical, mental/verbal, sexual, and financial abuse. ALL abuse must be reported immediately.

Any act that causes physical harm or injury to a resident. Examples include hitting, slapping, pinching, kicking, force-feeding, or improper use of physical or chemical restraints. CNAs must never participate in or witness physical abuse without reporting it.

Oral, written, or gestured language that includes threats, humiliation, harassment, or ridicule and causes a resident mental anguish or distress. Examples include yelling, swearing, threatening, or belittling a resident.

Non-consensual sexual contact of any kind with a resident, including touching, fondling, sexual coercion, or exposure. Also includes taking sexual photos of residents. Residents with dementia cannot legally consent to sexual activity.

Failure to provide goods and services necessary to avoid physical harm, mental anguish, or mental illness to a resident. Includes failure to provide adequate food, clothing, hygiene, medication, safety, or supervision. Both intentional and unintentional neglect must be reported.

The deliberate misplacement, exploitation, or wrongful use of a resident's personal belongings or money. Examples include stealing money, taking personal items, or using a resident's funds for personal gain.

Taking advantage of a resident for personal gain, including financial exploitation such as forging checks, coercing changes to a will, or misusing a power of attorney. CNAs must never accept money, gifts, or be named in a resident's will.
Separation of a resident from others or from their room against their will, or through coercion, as a means of punishment or convenience. This is a form of abuse and is prohibited.

An injury whose cause is not observed or is not consistent with the explanation provided. CNAs must document and report all such injuries immediately. The nursing home must investigate all injuries of unknown source.

A person required by law to report known or suspected abuse, neglect, or exploitation of vulnerable adults. All CNAs are mandatory reporters. Failure to report is a crime. Reports should be made to the supervisor and/or Adult Protective Services (APS).

Body system consisting of the heart and blood vessels that circulates blood throughout the body. The heart pumps oxygenated blood through arteries and receives deoxygenated blood through veins. Common disorders include hypertension, myocardial infarction, congestive heart failure, and angina.

A heart attack caused by blockage of a coronary artery, resulting in death of heart muscle tissue. Symptoms include crushing chest pain, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, and pain radiating to the left arm or jaw. A medical emergency — call 911 immediately.

A condition in which the heart is unable to pump enough blood to meet the body's needs, causing fluid to back up in the lungs and body tissues. Symptoms include shortness of breath, edema (especially in the legs/ankles), fatigue, and rapid weight gain.

Chest pain or pressure caused by reduced blood flow to the heart muscle, typically triggered by physical activity or stress. Unlike a heart attack, angina is temporary and does not cause permanent heart damage. Managed with rest and nitroglycerin.

A condition in which narrowed blood vessels reduce blood flow to the extremities. Symptoms include pain, cramping, or weakness in the legs with activity (claudication), cold or discolored skin, and slow-healing wounds. Serious risk of amputation if untreated.

Body system that brings oxygen into the body and removes carbon dioxide. Consists of the nose, pharynx, larynx, trachea, bronchi, bronchioles, and alveoli (air sacs in the lungs). Common disorders include pneumonia, asthma, emphysema, influenza, and tuberculosis.

An infection of one or both lungs caused by bacteria, viruses, or fungi, resulting in inflammation and fluid accumulation in the alveoli. Symptoms include fever, cough with colored mucus, shortness of breath, and chest pain. Common in elderly and immunocompromised residents.

A chronic respiratory condition characterized by episodes of airway inflammation, swelling, and bronchospasm that narrow the airways and make breathing difficult. Symptoms include wheezing, coughing, chest tightness, and shortness of breath. Triggered by allergens, exercise, or irritants.

A chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD) in which the air sacs (alveoli) are damaged and enlarged, reducing the lungs' ability to exchange oxygen and carbon dioxide. Primarily caused by smoking. Symptoms include chronic shortness of breath and barrel-shaped chest.

A highly contagious viral respiratory illness (the flu) spread through respiratory droplets. Symptoms include sudden onset of fever, chills, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, and respiratory symptoms. Prevented by annual vaccination. Can be life-threatening in elderly residents.

A contagious bacterial infection caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis, primarily affecting the lungs. Spread through airborne droplets. Symptoms include persistent cough (sometimes with blood), night sweats, weight loss, and fatigue. Requires airborne precautions (negative pressure room, N95 respirator).

Administration of supplemental oxygen to residents with hypoxia or respiratory distress. Delivered via nasal cannula (1-6 L/min), simple face mask, or non-rebreather mask. CNAs must never adjust oxygen flow rates without a nurse's order. Oxygen is flammable — no smoking or open flames near oxygen.

A device used to deliver supplemental oxygen through two small prongs inserted into the nostrils. The most common oxygen delivery device, providing low-flow oxygen at 1-6 liters per minute. CNAs check that prongs are correctly positioned and that tubing is not kinked.

The pulse measured at the radial artery on the inner wrist (thumb side). Counted for 60 seconds (or 30 seconds x2 if regular). Normal adult pulse: 60-100 beats per minute. Report a rate below 60 or above 100, or an irregular rhythm, to the nurse immediately.

The pattern or regularity of heartbeats. A regular rhythm has equal intervals between beats. An irregular (arrhythmic) rhythm has uneven intervals and must be reported to the nurse. When an irregular pulse is detected, the apical pulse should be taken for a full 60 seconds.

A table that slides over the bed by sliding its base underneath. Used by residents for meal trays, writing, reading, and other activities. Must be cleaned before and after use. Never place bedpans, urinals, or soiled linen on an overbed table.

A storage unit next to the resident's bed with a drawer and two shelves. Top drawer holds eyeglasses, books, and personal items. First shelf holds the wash basin and personal care items (soap, lotion, deodorant). The lower shelf holds the bedpan, urinal cover, and toilet paper.

A curtain pulled around the resident's bed while care is given to prevent others from seeing the resident. Privacy curtains provide visual privacy but do NOT block sound or prevent conversations from being heard. Providing visual privacy is a legal right of all residents.

Federal law enacted in 1987 that sets the minimum standards for nursing facility care. OBRA requires that resident rooms be as homelike as possible, that residents have the right to full visual privacy, the right to locked storage space, and the right to have and use personal items. OBRA also established the Resident Bill of Rights and requirements for CNA training and certification.

A type of isolation used to protect residents with weakened immune systems from germs in the environment, rather than to prevent the spread of infection from the resident. Used for residents who are immunocompromised, such as those receiving chemotherapy.

Donning means putting on personal protective equipment (PPE). Doffing means safely removing PPE. The correct order for donning PPE is: Gown → Mask → Gloves. The correct order for doffing PPE is: Gloves → Gown → Mask. This order prevents contamination of the face and hands. Wash hands after removing all PPE.

The stiffening of the body's muscles that occurs 2 to 4 hours after death. At this time the muscles become rigid, the joints stiffen, the blood ceases to circulate, and body temperature drops. It is important to align the body properly before rigor mortis occurs.

Care of the body after death. Can begin after the resident has been pronounced dead by a physician or licensed medical professional. Involves positioning the body supine, closing the eyes and mouth, removing jewelry, bathing soiled areas, placing a clean gown on the body, and gathering belongings. Must be performed with great care, empathy, and respect.

Care that focuses on relieving or reducing the intensity of uncomfortable symptoms without producing a cure. The intent is to improve quality of life and provide family support. Palliative care is for anyone with a long-term illness that will cause death, and can transition to hospice care.

Care that focuses on the physical, emotional, social, and spiritual needs of dying persons and their families. Usually for residents with less than 6 months to live. Cure or life-saving measures are not the concern — pain relief and comfort are stressed. Services include pain relief, comfort measures, spiritual needs, and bereavement care for the family.

An illness or injury from which the person will not likely recover — the disease or injury ends in death. Recovery is not expected. Doctors cannot predict the exact time of death — a person may have days, months, weeks, or years to live.

Five stages of dying described by Dr. Elizabeth Kubler-Ross, also called the stages of grief: Stage 1: Denial ('No, not me!'), Stage 2: Anger ('Why me?'), Stage 3: Bargaining ('Yes, me but...'), Stage 4: Depression ('Yes, me'), Stage 5: Acceptance (calm and at peace). Dying persons do not always pass through each stage and may move between stages.
Pain that is felt suddenly from injury, disease, trauma, or surgery. There is tissue damage. Acute pain lasts a short time (usually less than 6 months) and decreases with healing.

Pain that lasts longer than 6 months. Pain is constant or occurs off and on. There is no longer tissue damage and pain remains long after healing. Arthritis and cancer are common causes of chronic pain.

The degeneration, or wearing down, of the cartilage between two bones. Commonly occurs in the fingers, knees, hips, and spine. Causes include age, joint injury, and obesity. Signs and symptoms include pain and aching at the joint, weakness, muscle wasting, and a grating or cracking sound with motion of the joint.

The loss of bone mass, causing bones to become porous and brittle. Causes include calcium depletion due to immobility, dietary deficiencies of vitamin D and calcium, and estrogen deficiencies due to menopause. Signs include loss of height, hunchback, scoliosis (S-shaped curvature of the spine), fatigue, pain, and bone fractures.

A condition in which the pancreas fails to secrete enough insulin to handle the sugar created by the breakdown of foods. Glucose remains in the bloodstream instead of getting into the cells. Signs include extreme thirst, excessive hunger, frequent urination, sugar in the urine, irritability, blurred vision, slow healing of sores, and fatigue. Complications include hypoglycemia (low blood sugar) and hyperglycemia (high blood sugar).

Low blood sugar. Can result from too little food, too much insulin in the blood, diabetes medication, or heavy exercise. Signs and symptoms include hunger, perspiration, trembling, anxiety, headache, paleness, cold and clammy feeling, rapid heartbeat, sudden change in behavior or irritability, blurred or double vision, faintness, weakness, fatigue, mental confusion, and loss of consciousness.

High blood sugar. Can result from undiagnosed diabetes, too much food, too little insulin, not enough exercise, illness, or stress. Signs and symptoms include extreme thirst and frequent urination, labored and rapid breathing, breath that smells sweet or fruity, blurred vision, flushed cheeks, low blood pressure, mental confusion, nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain.

Occurs when blood flow to the brain is interrupted, either by a blood clot blocking a vessel or a burst blood vessel (hemorrhage). Brain cells in the affected area are deprived of oxygen and nutrients causing damage. If a stroke occurs on the right side of the brain, it affects the left side of the body, and vice versa. Use FAST to identify: Face drooping, Arm weakness, Speech difficulty, Time to call 911.

A progressive disorder of the nervous system affecting movement. Persons over the age of 50 are at risk. The myelin covering nerve impulses in the brain deteriorates. Signs include pill-rolling tremors in the hands, rigid and stiff muscles in the arms, legs, neck, and trunk, stooped posture with impaired balance, mask-like facial expression (cannot blink or smile), and slow monotone speech. Late signs include swallowing problems, constipation, depression, and memory loss.

A central nervous system disease in which the myelin covering nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord is destroyed (hardening or scarring). Nerve impulses are not sent to and from the brain normally. Symptoms usually start between ages 20 and 40 and include blurred or double vision, muscle weakness, tingling or numb sensations, partial or complete paralysis, balance problems, tremors, depression, bladder problems, and fatigue.

Violent and sudden contractions or tremors of muscle groups caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Movements are uncontrolled and the person may lose consciousness. Types include partial seizures (only one part of the brain involved), generalized tonic-clonic (grand mal — two phases: tonic with rigid muscles, then clonic with jerking and twitching), and generalized absence (petit mal — lasts a few seconds with brief loss of consciousness).

The prolonged retention and buildup of feces in the rectum. Feces are hard or putty-like. Results if constipation is not relieved. The person cannot have a bowel movement. Liquid feces pass around the hardened fecal mass in the rectum and seep from the anus — this can look like diarrhea. Signs include abdominal discomfort, distention, nausea, cramping, and rectal pain.

A chronic condition in which the liquid contents of the stomach back up into the esophagus. The liquid can inflame and damage the lining of the esophagus, causing bleeding or ulcers. Signs include heartburn at least twice per week, sour taste in the mouth, difficulty swallowing (dysphagia), feeling a lump in the throat, hoarseness, sore throat, dry cough, and regurgitating food or stomach acid.

A disorder that occurs in men as they age where the prostate becomes enlarged. This causes pressure on the urethra, leading to frequent urination, dribbling, difficulty starting the flow of urine, and urinary retention. Can cause urinary tract infections and kidney damage if untreated. BPH can be treated with medication or surgery.

A neat, secure method of tucking bed linens at the corners of the mattress to keep them tight and smooth. Used when making both occupied and unoccupied beds. A properly mitered corner prevents loose linens that can cause skin irritation or injury.
Routine personal care given before breakfast to prepare the resident for the day; includes oral hygiene, washing, hair care, and positioning.
Care given at bedtime (hour of sleep) to promote comfort and relaxation before sleep; includes hygiene, linen change, and back massage.
Hair loss that may be complete or partial; caused by heredity, cancer treatments, stress, poor nutrition, certain drugs, or hormone changes.
Infestation with lice — wingless insects that attach eggs (nits) to hair shafts; spread through shared items and treated with medicated shampoo.
Excessive shedding of dry, white flakes from the scalp, often with itching; corrected with medicated shampoos.
Mouth care that keeps the mouth and teeth clean, prevents odors and infection, and reduces risk of cavities and periodontal disease.
Gum disease caused by plaque and tartar buildup; leads to red, swollen, bleeding gums, bone destruction, and tooth loss.
A thin film of saliva, microbes, and other substances that sticks to teeth and causes tooth decay (cavities).
Hardened plaque that builds up at the gum line; causes periodontal disease and gum inflammation.
Breathing fluid, food, vomitus, or an object into the lungs; can cause pneumonia and death; a key risk for unconscious residents.
An artificial tooth or set of artificial teeth (false teeth) that replace missing teeth due to gum disease, decay, or injury.
A removable dental appliance that replaces missing teeth when some natural teeth remain.
A foot doctor who specializes in foot care; nursing assistants must not cut or trim toenails — this is the podiatrist's role.
A nail that grows into the surrounding skin, causing pain and potential infection; a portal of entry for microbes.
Death of body tissue, usually due to poor blood supply or infection; a serious complication of foot injuries in residents with circulatory disorders or diabetes.
The weaker side of the body due to stroke or injury. When dressing, place clothing on the affected side first; when undressing, remove from the stronger side first.
An artificial body part or self-help device used when a resident has difficulty performing an activity of daily living, such as an artificial limb, hearing aid, or glasses.
One of two tubes that carry urine from the kidneys to the bladder.
The tube through which urine passes out of the body from the bladder.
Scant or abnormally small production of urine; from 'olig' (scant) + 'uria' (urine).
Difficult or painful urination; from 'dys' (difficult) + 'uria' (urine). A common symptom of urinary tract infections.
The presence of blood in the urine; from 'hemat' (blood) + 'uria' (urine). May indicate UTI, trauma, or kidney disease.
Frequent urination during the night; a common age-related change in the urinary system.
Chronic Kidney Disease; gradual loss of kidney function over many years. Common causes include hypertension and diabetes.
The time when a female permanently stops having menstrual periods; associated with decreased estrogen levels which can lead to bone loss.
An infection of the vagina caused by bacteria, protozoa, or fungus (yeast). Signs include change in vaginal discharge, itching, and burning.
An indwelling urinary catheter that is inserted and left in the bladder so urine drains constantly into a drainage bag; held in place by an inflated balloon.
An artificial opening created surgically; for example, the opening created for a colostomy on the abdominal wall.
The surgical creation of an artificial opening (stoma) between the colon and the abdominal wall to allow feces to exit the body.
Mucus that is produced by the respiratory tract (lungs, bronchi, trachea) and expelled through the mouth; collected for specimen analysis.
A urine specimen collected after cleaning the perineal area to reduce the number of microbes in the sample; used for urinalysis to detect infections.
The introduction of fluid into the rectum and lower colon, ordered by a doctor to remove feces or relieve constipation or fecal impaction.
Cleaning the genital and anal areas; performed at least daily during bathing, or whenever the area is soiled, to prevent infection and promote comfort.
A portable toilet chair with a container used by residents who cannot walk to the bathroom; allows a normal position for elimination.
The measurement of all fluids taken in (intake) and all fluids lost (output) by a resident; used to monitor fluid balance.
A chemical substance produced by a gland and secreted into the bloodstream to control and regulate specific body functions.
The body's ability to maintain stable internal conditions despite changes in the external environment.
Underactivity of the thyroid gland, causing the body's normal rate of functioning to slow, resulting in mental and physical sluggishness.
Low blood sugar; occurs when there is too much insulin in the bloodstream. Symptoms include hunger, trembling, cold and clammy skin, rapid heartbeat, and mental confusion.
High blood sugar; occurs with too much sugar in the blood. Symptoms include extreme thirst, frequent urination, fruity breath, and mental confusion.
A condition in which the body fails to properly use the insulin it produces; the hallmark of Type 2 diabetes.
Swelling caused by excess fluid in body tissues; occurs when fluid intake exceeds fluid output. Common in people with heart and kidney disease.
A dangerous decrease in body water content, caused when fluid output exceeds fluid intake. Signs include dry skin, sunken eyes, dark urine, confusion, and fatigue.
Nothing by mouth (nil per os); a dietary order that prohibits any oral intake of food, liquids, or medications.
A special diet ordered by a physician to treat a disease, nutritional deficiency, or other health condition, or to eliminate/reduce certain substances from the diet.
Difficulty swallowing; refers to any problem in the swallowing process from mouth to stomach. Can lead to aspiration and pneumonia.
The accidental entry of food, liquid, or other foreign material into the lungs instead of the esophagus; a serious risk for residents with dysphagia.
A method of providing nutrients through the gastrointestinal tract via a feeding tube when a resident cannot chew or swallow.
Percutaneous Endoscopic Gastrostomy tube; a feeding tube surgically placed directly into the stomach through the abdominal wall.
The outermost layer of the skin that contains the pigment giving skin its color; acts as the first line of defense against the environment.
The inner layer of the skin containing connective tissue, blood vessels, nerve fibers, sweat glands, and oil glands.
The deepest layer of skin, also known as the fatty layer; helps the skin look smooth and acts as insulation.
A localized injury to the skin and/or underlying tissue, usually over a bony prominence, caused by unrelieved pressure, friction, or shear.
A breakdown of the skin caused by fluid buildup from poor vein function (venous insufficiency); commonly found on the ankle.
The IV administration of a highly concentrated solution of proteins, carbohydrates, vitamins, minerals, and fat; more nutritious than a regular IV solution.
The wasting away or decrease in size of a body organ or tissue due to lack of use or disease.
The degeneration or wearing down of the cartilage between two bones, commonly occurring in the fingers, knees, hips and spine.
The loss of bone mass, causing the bones to become porous and brittle, increasing the risk of fractures.
A broken bone. Fractures may be simple (one place), open/compound (bone through skin), or closed (bone broken, skin intact).
A treatment that uses a steady pull from two directions (using weights, ropes and pulleys) to reduce and immobilize fractures.
The way in which the parts of the body work together when a person moves, designed to avoid muscle strain and prevent injury.
The area beneath a person that includes all points of contact with the supporting surface. A wide base of support increases balance and stability.
The permanent shortening of a muscle or joint that results in a deformity, typically caused by prolonged immobility or lack of range of motion exercises.
A belt placed around a resident's waist and used by the CNA to assist with transfers and ambulation safely, preventing arm and shoulder dislocation.
A semi-sitting position where the head of the bed is raised. Low Fowler's: 15–45°; Semi Fowler's: 60°; High Fowler's: 90°.
A semi-prone side-lying position with the upper leg more flexed. Used to relieve pressure from the sacrum and heels, and for enema administration.
A side-lying position used for sleeping, rotating, and relieving pressure from bony prominences. Contraindicated for residents with severe spinal disease or hip fractures.
Paralysis on one side of the body, often caused by a stroke (CVA). The affected side is opposite to the side of the brain where the stroke occurred.
Cerebrovascular Accident — commonly called a stroke. Occurs when blood supply to part of the brain is interrupted, causing brain cell death and loss of function.
A loss or impairment of the ability to communicate through speech, writing, or signs, often caused by stroke or brain injury.
Violent and sudden contractions or tremors of muscle groups caused by abnormal electrical activity in the brain. Types include partial, grand mal, and petit mal.
A central nervous system disease in which the myelin covering of nerve fibers in the brain and spinal cord is destroyed, impairing nerve impulse transmission.
A progressive neurological disorder affecting movement, characterized by tremors, rigid muscles, stooped posture, and mask-like facial expression.
The ability to walk or move about on foot. CNAs assist residents with ambulation to prevent complications of immobility and promote independence.
A triangular pillow placed between the legs after hip surgery to immobilize and position the hips and knees, preventing the hip from being turned inward or outward.

The organ system that forms the external covering of the body, consisting of the skin, hair, nails, and associated glands. It protects the body from the environment, regulates temperature, prevents water loss, and provides sensory information.

The body system made up of muscles and bones that provides the framework for the body and allows it to move. Includes 206 bones and approximately 500 muscles in the adult body, as well as joints, cartilage, and tendons.
The body system that controls, directs, and coordinates body functions. Divided into the Central Nervous System (brain and spinal cord) and the Peripheral Nervous System (cranial and spinal nerves).
The division of the nervous system consisting of the brain and spinal cord. It receives, processes, and responds to sensory information from the body.
The division of the nervous system consisting of 12 pairs of cranial nerves and 31 pairs of spinal nerves. It carries impulses between the central nervous system and the rest of the body.
The body system made up of glands that produce and secrete hormones directly into the bloodstream. It regulates growth, metabolism, reproduction, blood sugar levels, and maintains homeostasis.

The body system responsible for breaking down food into nutrients that can be absorbed into the bloodstream and used by the body. Includes the mouth, esophagus, stomach, small intestine, large intestine, and accessory organs.
The body system responsible for filtering waste products from the blood and eliminating them from the body as urine. Consists of the kidneys, ureters, bladder, and urethra.

The body system responsible for producing offspring. The male reproductive system produces and delivers sperm; the female reproductive system produces eggs and provides the environment for fetal development.

A restorative nursing technique in which a resident is taught to use a stronger or unaffected body part to compensate for a weaker or impaired one, thereby maintaining as much independence as possible in activities of daily living.
Surgical removal or excision of a body part or structure. Example: appendectomy (removal of the appendix), tonsillectomy (removal of the tonsils), mastectomy (removal of the breast).
Surgical incision into a body part; to cut into. Example: tracheotomy (incision into the trachea), laparotomy (incision into the abdomen), craniotomy (incision into the skull).

Surgical creation of an artificial opening between an organ and the body surface or between two organs. Example: colostomy (opening from colon to skin), ileostomy (opening from ileum to skin), tracheostomy (permanent opening in the trachea).

Surgical repair, reconstruction, or reshaping of a body part. Example: rhinoplasty (surgical repair of the nose), arthroplasty (surgical reconstruction of a joint), mammoplasty (surgical reshaping of the breast).
Surgical suturing or stitching of a wound or body part. Example: herniorrhaphy (suturing of a hernia), cardiorrhaphy (suturing of the heart), perineorrhaphy (suturing of the perineum).

Surgical binding, fusion, or fixation of a joint or structure. Example: arthrodesis (surgical fusion of a joint), pleurodesis (fusion of the pleural layers), tenodesis (surgical fixation of a tendon).

Surgical fixation or suspension of an organ to hold it in place. Example: orchiopexy (fixation of an undescended testicle), nephropexy (surgical fixation of a floating kidney), mastopexy (breast lift surgery).
Crushing or breaking of a structure, often a stone or calculus. Example: lithotripsy (crushing of kidney stones), cholecystolithotripsy (crushing of gallstones).

Surgical puncture of a cavity or organ to aspirate (withdraw) fluid. Example: amniocentesis (puncture of the amniotic sac), thoracentesis (puncture of the chest cavity), arthrocentesis (puncture of a joint).
Visual examination using an instrument (scope). Example: endoscopy (visual exam of the inside of the body), bronchoscopy (exam of the airways), colonoscopy (exam of the colon).

An instrument used to visually examine a body part or cavity. Example: stethoscope (instrument to listen to heart/lung sounds), otoscope (instrument to examine the ear), ophthalmoscope (instrument to examine the eye).
The process of recording or producing an image of a body structure. Example: radiography (X-ray imaging), echocardiography (ultrasound of the heart), mammography (X-ray of the breast).

A record, image, or tracing produced by a diagnostic test or instrument. Example: electrocardiogram (ECG - tracing of heart electrical activity), mammogram (X-ray image of the breast), angiogram (image of blood vessels).

An instrument used to measure a specific quantity or value. Example: thermometer (instrument to measure temperature), sphygmomanometer (instrument to measure blood pressure), spirometer (instrument to measure lung capacity).
The process or science of measuring something. Example: spirometry (measuring lung capacity), audiometry (measuring hearing), optometry (measuring visual acuity).

Inflammation of a tissue or organ. Example: appendicitis (inflammation of the appendix), arthritis (inflammation of joints), dermatitis (inflammation of the skin), bronchitis (inflammation of the bronchi).

A condition, process, or abnormal increase - often describing a disease state or pathological process. Example: fibrosis (formation of excess fibrous tissue), cyanosis (bluish discoloration), psychosis (a mental disorder involving loss of reality).

A condition of the blood; refers to the presence or level of a substance in the blood. Example: anemia (insufficient red blood cells), hyperglycemia (high blood glucose), bacteremia (bacteria in the bloodstream), septicemia (infection in the bloodstream).
Pain in a specific body part or region. Example: neuralgia (nerve pain), myalgia (muscle pain), arthralgia (joint pain), cephalgia (headache).
Pain; used interchangeably with -algia in many terms. Example: mastodynia (breast pain), pleurodynia (chest/rib muscle pain), gastrodynia (stomach pain).
Disease or disorder of a body part or system. Example: neuropathy (disease of the nerves), cardiomyopathy (disease of the heart muscle), nephropathy (disease of the kidneys).

Abnormal enlargement of a body organ or part. Example: cardiomegaly (enlarged heart), splenomegaly (enlarged spleen), hepatomegaly (enlarged liver), acromegaly (enlargement of extremities due to excess growth hormone).

A hernia, cyst, or abnormal protrusion of an organ through surrounding tissue. Example: hydrocele (fluid-filled sac around the testicle), cystocele (herniation of the bladder into the vaginal wall), rectocele (herniation of the rectum).
Dilation, expansion, or stretching of a hollow organ or vessel. Example: bronchiectasis (abnormal dilation of the bronchi), telangiectasis (dilation of small blood vessels near the skin surface).

Narrowing or constriction of a passage, vessel, or opening. Example: aortic stenosis (narrowing of the aortic valve), spinal stenosis (narrowing of the spinal canal), pyloric stenosis (narrowing of the pylorus).

Destruction, breakdown, dissolution, or loosening of cells or tissue. Example: hemolysis (destruction of red blood cells), dialysis (mechanical filtration of waste from blood), paralysis (loss of muscle function).

Drooping, prolapse, or downward displacement of an organ or body part. Example: blepharoptosis (drooping of the eyelid), nephroptosis (downward displacement of the kidney), visceroptosis (prolapse of abdominal organs).

Sudden, involuntary contraction or cramping of a muscle or hollow organ. Example: bronchospasm (sudden contraction of airway muscles), vasospasm (sudden constriction of a blood vessel), laryngospasm (sudden closure of the vocal cords).

Paralysis or loss of voluntary movement in a body region. Example: hemiplegia (paralysis of one side of the body), paraplegia (paralysis of the lower body), quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs).
Partial or incomplete paralysis; weakness in voluntary movement. Example: hemiparesis (weakness on one side of the body), gastroparesis (partial paralysis of stomach muscles).
Deficiency or abnormal reduction in the number of cells or a substance. Example: leukopenia (low white blood cell count), thrombocytopenia (low platelet count), osteopenia (reduced bone density).

Stopping, controlling, slowing, or maintaining a steady state of a bodily process. Example: hemostasis (stopping of bleeding), bacteriostasis (inhibition of bacterial growth), homeostasis (maintenance of a stable internal environment).

Relating to nourishment, development, or growth of tissue. Example: atrophy (wasting away or shrinkage of tissue), hypertrophy (excessive growth of tissue), dystrophy (abnormal or defective development).
Vomiting or the act of expelling stomach contents through the mouth. Example: hematemesis (vomiting blood), hyperemesis (excessive vomiting), antiemetic (medication to prevent vomiting).

Flow, discharge, or excessive secretion from a body structure. Example: diarrhea (excessive loose stool), rhinorrhea (runny nose - nasal discharge), menorrhea (menstrual flow), otorrhea (discharge from the ear).
Excessive or abnormal bleeding or hemorrhage from a body part. Example: menorrhagia (heavy menstrual bleeding), hemorrhage (excessive bleeding), otorrhagia (bleeding from the ear).

An abnormal, persistent, and irrational fear of a specific object, situation, or activity. Example: claustrophobia (fear of enclosed spaces), agoraphobia (fear of open or crowded spaces), acrophobia (fear of heights).

The origin, production, development, or formation of something. Example: pathogenesis (origin and development of a disease), carcinogenesis (development of cancer), hematopoiesis (formation of blood cells).

Producing, originating from, or caused by a specific source. Example: carcinogenic (cancer-causing), iatrogenic (caused by medical treatment), psychogenic (originating in the mind), pyrogenic (fever-producing).

Attraction to, abnormal love of, or tendency toward a specific substance or condition; also used to indicate a clotting affinity. Example: hemophilia (tendency to bleed excessively due to clotting disorder).

Full of, resembling, having the nature of, or abundantly containing a substance. In chemistry, -ose denotes a sugar or carbohydrate. Example: adipose (full of fat tissue), glucose (a simple sugar), sucrose (table sugar), verbose (full of words).

Resembling, like, or having the appearance or form of. Example: deltoid (triangular muscle, resembling the Greek letter delta), opioid (resembling opium in its effects), sigmoid (S-shaped, resembling the letter sigma).

Pertaining to, relating to, or of. One of the most common adjectival suffixes in medical terminology. Example: renal (pertaining to the kidneys), femoral (pertaining to the femur), spinal (pertaining to the spine).
Pertaining to, having the nature of, or relating to. Example: gastric (pertaining to the stomach), hepatic (pertaining to the liver), systemic (pertaining to the whole body system).

Having, full of, or characterized by a quality or substance. Example: cancerous (having the quality of cancer), mucous (relating to mucus), venous (pertaining to veins), nervous (pertaining to nerves).
Relating to, connected with, or belonging to. Example: pulmonary (pertaining to the lungs), urinary (pertaining to urine/urination), coronary (pertaining to the arteries of the heart).
Pertaining to a position, direction, or anatomical location. Example: anterior (toward the front), posterior (toward the back), superior (above), inferior (below).

The study of, branch of knowledge about, or science of a particular subject. Example: cardiology (study of the heart), dermatology (study of the skin), neurology (study of the nervous system), oncology (study of cancer).

A specialist or expert in a particular field of study or medicine. Example: cardiologist (heart specialist), neurologist (nervous system specialist), dermatologist (skin specialist), oncologist (cancer specialist).
Relating to urine, urination, or a condition of the urine. Example: hematuria (blood in urine), polyuria (excessive urination), dysuria (painful urination), glycosuria (glucose in urine).
Eating, swallowing, or an abnormal desire to eat a specific substance. Example: dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), polyphagia (excessive eating - a sign of diabetes), aphagia (inability to swallow).
Breathing or a condition related to breathing. Example: dyspnea (difficulty breathing), apnea (absence of breathing), tachypnea (abnormally rapid breathing), bradypnea (abnormally slow breathing).
Condition or rate relating to the heart. Example: tachycardia (abnormally fast heart rate over 100 bpm), bradycardia (abnormally slow heart rate under 60 bpm).
Speech or a condition of speech or language. Example: aphasia (inability to speak or understand language, often from brain injury), dysphasia (difficulty with speech).

A tumor, mass, or abnormal growth of tissue - may be benign or malignant depending on context. Example: carcinoma (malignant tumor of epithelial cells), melanoma (malignant tumor of pigment-producing cells), lipoma (benign fatty tumor).
A cell of a specific type. Example: erythrocyte (red blood cell), leukocyte (white blood cell), thrombocyte (platelet), osteocyte (bone cell).

An immature, precursor, or primitive cell that will develop into a more specialized cell. Example: osteoblast (bone-forming cell), fibroblast (connective tissue cell), erythroblast (immature red blood cell).

An enzyme that catalyzes a chemical reaction, usually breaking down a specific substrate. Example: lipase (enzyme that breaks down fats), amylase (enzyme that breaks down starch), lactase (enzyme that breaks down lactose).
Without, absence of, or lacking. Example: apnea (without breathing), anemia (without sufficient blood/iron), aphasia (without speech), asepsis (without infection).
Slow. Example: bradycardia (slow heart rate below 60 bpm), bradypnea (slow breathing rate below 12 breaths/min), bradykinesia (slowness of movement, seen in Parkinson's disease).
Rapid or fast. Example: tachycardia (fast heart rate above 100 bpm), tachypnea (rapid breathing rate above 20 breaths/min).
Above normal, excessive, or elevated. Example: hypertension (high blood pressure), hyperglycemia (high blood glucose), hyperthyroidism (overactive thyroid), hyperventilation (excessive breathing).

Below normal, deficient, or decreased. Example: hypotension (low blood pressure), hypoglycemia (low blood glucose), hypothyroidism (underactive thyroid), hypothermia (abnormally low body temperature).
Many, much, or excessive. Example: polyuria (excessive urination - a sign of diabetes), polyphagia (excessive hunger), polydipsia (excessive thirst), polyneuropathy (disease affecting many nerves).
Few, scanty, or deficient. Example: oliguria (scant urine output less than 400 mL/day), oligomenorrhea (infrequent menstruation), oligodendroglia (few supporting brain cells).
Difficult, painful, abnormal, or impaired. Example: dyspnea (difficulty breathing), dysphagia (difficulty swallowing), dysuria (painful urination), dysfunction (abnormal function).
Half or one side. Example: hemiplegia (paralysis of one side of the body), hemiparesis (weakness on one side), hemigastrectomy (removal of half the stomach).
Around, surrounding, or near. Example: pericardium (the sac surrounding the heart), perioperative (around the time of surgery), perineal (area around the anus and genitals).
Within, inside, or inner. Example: endocrine (secreting internally into the bloodstream), endoscopy (visual exam inside the body), endotracheal (within the trachea).
Upon, above, or over. Example: epidermis (outer layer of skin, above the dermis), epidural (above the dura - outer brain/spinal cord covering), epigastric (above the stomach).
Under, below, or less than. Example: subcutaneous (under the skin), sublingual (under the tongue), subclavian (under the clavicle/collarbone), subnormal (below normal).
Above or over. Example: suprapubic (above the pubic bone), supraventricular (above the ventricles), suprarenal (above the kidneys - another name for adrenal glands).
Within or inside. Example: intravenous (within a vein - IV), intramuscular (within a muscle - IM injection), intracranial (within the skull), intrauterine (within the uterus).
Between or among. Example: intercostal (between the ribs), intervertebral (between the vertebrae), intermittent (occurring between periods of normal activity).
Across, through, or beyond. Example: transdermal (through the skin - e.g., medication patches), transfusion (transfer of blood across vessels), transient (passing through briefly).
Before, in front of, or prior to. Example: preoperative (before surgery), prenatal (before birth), preeclampsia (condition before eclampsia), premature (before the expected time).
After, behind, or following. Example: postoperative (after surgery), postmortem (after death), postnatal (after birth), post-traumatic (after a traumatic event).
New or recent. Example: neonate (a newborn infant - first 28 days of life), neoplasm (new/abnormal growth of tissue - a tumor), neonatal (relating to the newborn period).
Small or microscopic. Example: microorganism (organism too small to see without a microscope), microbiology (study of microscopic organisms), microvascular (relating to very small blood vessels).
Large or long. Example: macrocyte (abnormally large red blood cell), macroscopic (visible to the naked eye), macronutrients (large nutritional components - carbohydrates, fats, proteins).

Bad, abnormal, or poorly. Example: malnutrition (poor/inadequate nutrition), malignant (bad - refers to cancer that spreads), malaise (general feeling of being unwell), malpractice (improper practice).
Against, opposing, or preventing. Example: antibiotic (against bacterial life), antiemetic (against vomiting), antiseptic (against infection/sepsis), anticoagulant (against blood clotting).
Self or same individual. Example: autoimmune (immune system attacking self), autograft (tissue transplanted from one's own body), autopsy (examination of self - examination after death).
Two or double. Example: bilateral (on both sides), binocular (using both eyes), bifurcation (splitting into two branches), bicuspid (having two cusps).
One or single. Example: unilateral (on one side only), unicellular (single-celled), unipolar (having one pole or process).

Tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchioles in the lungs where gas exchange occurs — oxygen enters the blood and carbon dioxide is released. Damage to alveoli (as in emphysema) reduces the surface area for gas exchange.
The windpipe; a tube approximately 4-5 inches long that carries air from the larynx to the bronchi. It is located in front of the esophagus and contains C-shaped rings of cartilage to keep it open.
The two main branches of the trachea that lead into the left and right lungs. They further branch into smaller bronchioles. Inflammation of the bronchi is called bronchitis.
The voice box; located between the pharynx and trachea. Contains the vocal cords and produces sound for speech. The epiglottis covers the larynx during swallowing to prevent aspiration.
The throat; a muscular tube that serves as a common passageway for both air (to the larynx/trachea) and food (to the esophagus). Divided into the nasopharynx, oropharynx, and laryngopharynx.

The dome-shaped muscle below the lungs that is the primary muscle of respiration. When it contracts, it flattens and pulls air into the lungs (inhalation). When it relaxes, air is pushed out (exhalation).
The muscular tube approximately 10 inches long that carries food and liquid from the throat (pharynx) to the stomach using wave-like contractions called peristalsis. It is located behind the trachea.

A dual-function gland located behind the stomach. As an endocrine gland, it produces insulin and glucagon to regulate blood sugar. As an exocrine gland, it produces digestive enzymes (amylase, lipase, protease) released into the small intestine.

The largest internal organ, located in the upper right abdomen. Produces bile for fat digestion, filters toxins from the blood, metabolizes drugs and alcohol, stores glycogen, and produces clotting factors. The liver has remarkable regenerative ability.

A small pear-shaped organ beneath the liver that stores and concentrates bile produced by the liver. Bile is released into the small intestine during digestion to break down fats. Gallstones can form and block the bile duct.

The involuntary, wave-like muscular contractions of hollow organs (esophagus, stomach, intestines) that propel contents forward during digestion. Disruption of peristalsis can cause conditions like ileus or constipation.

The large intestine; approximately 5 feet long. Absorbs water and electrolytes from digestive waste and compacts it into feces. Divided into ascending, transverse, descending, and sigmoid sections, ending at the rectum.

The final section of the large intestine, approximately 5 inches long, that stores feces before elimination. Stretching of the rectal wall triggers the urge to defecate. Constipation or fecal impaction can occur here.

A firm but flexible connective tissue found in joints (articular cartilage), the nose, ears, larynx, trachea, and between vertebrae (intervertebral discs). In osteoarthritis, the cartilage covering joint surfaces gradually wears away.

Dense, fibrous connective tissue that attaches muscle to bone. Tendons transmit the force of muscle contraction to move bones. They can be strained (overstretched) or ruptured (torn). Example: the Achilles tendon connects the calf muscle to the heel bone.

Dense, fibrous connective tissue that connects bone to bone, stabilizing joints. Ligaments can be sprained (stretched or torn) from sudden force. Example: the ACL (anterior cruciate ligament) stabilizes the knee joint.

One of the 33 bones that make up the spinal column (spine/backbone). Vertebrae protect the spinal cord, support the skull, and allow movement. They are grouped as cervical (7), thoracic (12), lumbar (5), sacral (5 fused), and coccygeal (4 fused).
A large triangular bone at the base of the spine, formed by five fused vertebrae. It connects the spine to the pelvis. The sacral area is a common site for pressure injuries in bedridden patients.

The breastbone; a flat, narrow bone in the center of the chest that connects to the ribs via cartilage. The sternum protects the heart and major blood vessels. CPR chest compressions are performed here.

The largest part of the brain, responsible for conscious thought, intelligence, memory, personality, sensation, and voluntary motor control. Divided into right and left hemispheres; each hemisphere controls the opposite side of the body.

The region of the brain at the back and bottom, responsible for coordinating voluntary movements, balance, posture, and fine motor control. Damage to the cerebellum causes unsteady gait and lack of coordination (ataxia).

The lower extension of the brain connecting to the spinal cord. Controls vital automatic functions including heart rate, breathing, blood pressure, swallowing, and consciousness. Divided into the midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata.

A cylindrical bundle of nerve tissue extending from the brain stem through the vertebral column. It carries motor signals from the brain to the body and sensory signals from the body to the brain. Injury can result in paralysis below the level of damage.

A specialized nerve cell that transmits electrical and chemical signals throughout the nervous system. Composed of a cell body, dendrites (receive signals), and an axon (sends signals). Neurons are the basic functional units of the brain and nervous system.

A hormone produced by the beta cells of the pancreas that allows glucose to enter body cells for energy. Without adequate insulin (or with insulin resistance), glucose builds up in the bloodstream, causing hyperglycemia and eventually diabetes mellitus.

A butterfly-shaped gland in the front of the neck that produces thyroid hormones (T3, T4) to regulate metabolism, energy, heart rate, and body temperature. Underactivity = hypothyroidism; overactivity = hyperthyroidism.

The primary female sex hormone produced mainly by the ovaries. Regulates the menstrual cycle, supports bone density, and maintains cardiovascular health. After menopause, estrogen levels drop significantly, increasing risk of osteoporosis and heart disease.

A network of vessels, lymph nodes, and organs (spleen, thymus) that drain excess fluid from tissues back into the blood, transport immune cells (lymphocytes), and filter pathogens. Swollen lymph nodes are a sign of infection or disease.

The three protective membranes surrounding the brain and spinal cord: the dura mater (outermost), arachnoid mater (middle), and pia mater (innermost). Inflammation of these membranes is called meningitis.

Any abnormal or irregular heart rhythm. Can range from harmless (e.g., occasional skipped beat) to life-threatening (e.g., ventricular fibrillation). Causes include heart disease, electrolyte imbalances, and stimulants. Report to nurse immediately.

A common cardiac arrhythmia in which the upper chambers (atria) beat chaotically and irregularly instead of in coordinated contractions. Increases risk of stroke due to blood pooling and clot formation. Often treated with blood thinners and rate-control medications.

A blood clot (thrombus) forming in a deep vein, typically in the leg. Risk factors include immobility, surgery, and dehydration. Symptoms include leg pain, swelling, and warmth. Dangerous if the clot travels to the lungs (pulmonary embolism). Prevention includes early ambulation, compression stockings, and hydration.

A life-threatening blockage of one or more pulmonary arteries in the lungs, most commonly caused by a blood clot that has traveled from a deep vein (DVT). Symptoms include sudden chest pain, shortness of breath, and rapid heart rate. This is a medical emergency.

Excessive forward curvature of the upper spine, causing a rounded or hunched back. Common in older adults, especially those with osteoporosis or vertebral compression fractures. Can impair breathing and mobility.

An abnormal lateral (sideways) S-shaped or C-shaped curvature of the spine. Mild cases may require only monitoring; severe cases can impair breathing and require bracing or surgery. More common in adolescent girls.

The accumulation of urea and other waste products in the blood due to kidney failure. Symptoms include nausea, vomiting, confusion, fatigue, and a characteristic ammonia smell on the breath. Requires dialysis or kidney transplant if severe.

A temporary episode of stroke-like symptoms caused by a brief interruption of blood flow to the brain, lasting minutes to hours with full recovery. Often called a 'mini-stroke' or 'warning stroke.' TIA is a major warning sign of an impending stroke and requires immediate medical evaluation.

A life-threatening medical emergency where the body's response to infection spirals out of control, damaging its own tissues and organs. Signs include fever or hypothermia, rapid heart rate, rapid breathing, and confusion. Requires immediate treatment with IV antibiotics and fluids.

A group of progressive lung diseases (primarily emphysema and chronic bronchitis) that obstruct airflow and make breathing difficult. Most commonly caused by long-term smoking. Symptoms include chronic cough, wheezing, and shortness of breath. Cannot be cured but can be managed.

An umbrella term for a group of symptoms affecting memory, thinking, and social abilities severely enough to interfere with daily life. Not a normal part of aging. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause. CNAs must use patience, consistent routines, and therapeutic communication when caring for patients with dementia.

The most common form of dementia, causing progressive memory loss and cognitive decline. Brain cells and connections gradually die. Stages progress from mild forgetfulness to complete dependence. No cure exists; care focuses on safety, routine, and quality of life.

A temporary loss of consciousness (fainting) caused by inadequate blood flow to the brain. Common causes include standing too quickly (orthostatic hypotension), dehydration, and cardiac arrhythmias. CNAs should ease patients to the floor safely and report immediately.

A sudden drop in blood pressure upon standing from a sitting or lying position, causing dizziness, lightheadedness, or fainting (syncope). Common in older adults and those on blood pressure medications. Prevention: have patients sit at the edge of the bed for 1-2 minutes before standing.

A bacterial skin infection of the deeper layers of skin and underlying tissue, typically caused by Staphylococcus or Streptococcus bacteria. Signs include redness, warmth, swelling, and tenderness. Commonly affects the legs. Can spread rapidly and requires antibiotic treatment.

A viral infection caused by the reactivation of the varicella-zoster virus (the same virus that causes chickenpox) lying dormant in nerve tissue. Produces a painful, blistering rash typically on one side of the body along a nerve path. Contagious to those who haven't had chickenpox. Requires contact precautions.

A form of inflammatory arthritis caused by the buildup of uric acid crystals in joints, most commonly the big toe. Causes sudden, severe pain, redness, and swelling. Triggered by high-purine foods (red meat, alcohol, shellfish). Treated with anti-inflammatory medications and dietary changes.

A chronic autoimmune disease in which the immune system attacks the synovial membranes lining the joints, causing inflammation, pain, swelling, and eventual joint destruction. Unlike osteoarthritis, RA is systemic and can affect organs. Often causes symmetric joint involvement (both hands, both knees).

The surgical or traumatic removal of a limb or part of a limb. May be required due to severe peripheral vascular disease, diabetes complications, trauma, or cancer. CNAs assist with stump care, positioning, and supporting patients adjusting to prosthetic devices.

Clear or pale yellow, watery wound drainage composed mainly of plasma. This is normal during the early stages of wound healing and indicates the wound is responding appropriately. Document color, amount, and characteristics.

Thin, pink or pale red wound drainage that is a mixture of serum (clear fluid) and a small amount of blood. This is normal in the early healing stages. Report any change to darker red color, which may indicate increased bleeding.
Bright red, bloody wound drainage indicating active bleeding or a highly vascular wound. Small amounts are normal in new wounds. Large or increasing amounts must be reported immediately to the nurse.

Thick, opaque wound drainage that is yellow, green, tan, or brown — typically with an unpleasant odor. Indicates infection and the presence of bacteria and dead white blood cells (pus). Must be reported immediately to the nurse.

A mechanical force in which layers of skin and tissue slide against each other in opposite directions, stretching and tearing the blood vessels that supply the skin. Occurs when a patient slides down in bed or is dragged across a surface. A major contributing factor to pressure injuries.

The mechanical rubbing force between two surfaces — typically the patient's skin and a bed surface or clothing. Unlike shear, friction affects only the surface layer of skin. Contributes to pressure injuries. Proper lifting/repositioning technique prevents friction damage.

A medical procedure that artificially filters waste products, excess fluid, and toxins from the blood when the kidneys can no longer do so. Hemodialysis uses an external machine; peritoneal dialysis uses the patient's own abdominal lining. CNAs assist with transport, monitoring fluid restrictions, and dietary support.

A laboratory test that analyzes the physical, chemical, and microscopic properties of urine to detect conditions such as urinary tract infections, kidney disease, and diabetes. CNAs are often responsible for collecting clean-catch urine specimens.

The insertion of a tube (endotracheal tube) into the trachea (airway) to maintain an open airway, deliver oxygen, or provide mechanical ventilation. Performed by a physician or respiratory therapist. Patients with endotracheal tubes cannot speak and require alternate communication methods.

A class of medications that relax and widen (dilate) the muscles surrounding the airways, making it easier to breathe. Commonly delivered via inhaler or nebulizer. Used to treat asthma and COPD. Examples include albuterol (Ventolin) and ipratropium (Atrovent).

A device that converts liquid medication into a fine mist that can be inhaled deep into the lungs. Commonly used for patients with asthma, COPD, or respiratory infections. CNAs may set up equipment and assist the patient, but medication administration is performed by licensed staff.

A handheld breathing device used after surgery or during illness to encourage deep breathing and help keep the alveoli (air sacs) inflated, preventing pneumonia and atelectasis. The patient inhales slowly and deeply to raise a marker to a target level. CNAs coach and encourage use as directed.

Inflatable sleeve-like devices placed on the legs that intermittently squeeze and release to promote blood flow and prevent deep vein thrombosis (DVT) in immobile patients. Also called pneumatic compression devices. CNAs apply, remove, and check skin condition underneath as directed.

A method of administering fluids, medications, nutrients, or blood directly into a vein via a needle or catheter. CNAs do not administer IV medications but must observe the IV site for redness, swelling, or leaking (infiltration) and report to the nurse.

A flexible tube inserted through the nose, down the esophagus, and into the stomach. Used to deliver liquid nutrition (tube feeding), administer medications, or remove stomach contents. CNAs may assist with tube feeding setup but not insertion/removal.

Elastic hosiery that applies graduated pressure to the legs, with the most pressure at the ankle decreasing toward the knee or thigh. Used to prevent DVT, reduce edema, and manage varicose veins. CNAs apply and remove these as directed, checking skin condition before application.

A mobile cart stocked with emergency resuscitation equipment and medications (defibrillator, oxygen, epinephrine, IV supplies) used during a medical emergency (code blue). CNAs should know the location of the code cart on their unit and call for help immediately in an emergency.

A high-pitched whistling or sighing sound produced when air flows through narrowed or obstructed airways. Heard most often during exhalation. Common in asthma, COPD, and anaphylaxis. Always report new or worsening wheezing to the nurse immediately.

An uncomfortable awareness of the heartbeat — the sensation that the heart is beating rapidly, irregularly, pounding, or skipping beats. Can be triggered by stress, caffeine, dehydration, or cardiac arrhythmias. Report to the nurse, especially if accompanied by chest pain or dizziness.

The partial or total loss of memory, often caused by brain injury, stroke, neurological disease, severe psychological trauma, or certain medications. Anterograde amnesia is the inability to form new memories after the event; retrograde amnesia is the loss of memories from before the event. CNAs should use calm, reassuring communication and avoid correcting or arguing with a person who cannot recall recent events.
